title: Streaming graceful shutdown and deadline negotiation for Go SDK
creator: Ethan Park
description: Problem: Current Go SDK streaming implementation has multiple cancellation and timeout footguns for customers: abrupt EOF on client.Cancel, goroutine leaks if server doesn't acknowledge, and inconsistent deadline semantics when SDK callers set timeouts on both the parent context and per-read operations. Goal: Design and implement a robust streaming API that gives callers explicit control over graceful shutdown vs. immediate cancel, negotiates a short 'drain' window with the server when possible, and documents clear semantics for deadline propagation so customers can avoid races.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New Stream type supports GracefulClose(ctx, drainTimeout) which requests server-side drain and waits up to drainTimeout for server to finish sending in-flight tokens. 2) Immediate Close(err) interrupts the stream without waiting. 3) SDK guarantees no goroutine leaks under cancellation and server disconnect scenarios (checked by unit/integration tests). 4) Context deadlines propagate only to network-level operations; per-message read timeouts can be set independently. 5) Backwards-compatible with existing generated clients: existing code that calls Stream.Close() should behave as immediate close by default.
design_decisions: - Expose a single Stream object with methods: Recv() (blocking), CloseImmediate(err error), GracefulClose(ctx context.Context, drain time.Duration) error, and WithReadDeadline(d time.Duration) to set per-read timeout. - Internally use a single background goroutine to read from the wire into a buffered channel; Recv() reads from that channel to avoid per-call network blocking. This permits CloseImmediate to cancel the reader via an internal cancel func and drain the channel according to policy. - Negotiation: when GracefulClose is called, the client sends a control frame (X-Drain: <ms>) to the server. If the server supports drain, it will stop accepting new work for this stream and flush. If not supported, server replies with 501 and client falls back to timed local drain. - Use context.Context for operation-wide cancellation and a separate child context for the inbound reader; this avoids races where a parent deadline cancels the reader while a Recv is in progress. - Avoid exposing internal channels to callers to reduce misuse. - Keep existing Close() behavior as alias for CloseImmediate to maintain compatibility.
implementation_notes: - Core types: type Stream struct { conn net.Conn; readerCtx context.Context; readerCancel context.CancelFunc; inbound chan *Message; mu sync.Mutex; closed atomic.Bool; readDeadline time.Duration } - Recv() respects the current readDeadline and returns (Message, nil) or (nil, ErrCanceled/ErrDeadline). - GracefulClose(ctx, drain) sends a small control frame and then waits on either: inbound channel drained OR ctx.Done() OR timer expired. - CloseImmediate(err) cancels readerCtx and close inbound channel; callers get ErrStreamClosed on subsequent Recv(). - Reconnection: Include a resume token in stream state. If a transient network error occurs and the server supports resume, client will attempt N retries with exponential backoff, preserving partial KV cache message offsets. - Tests: unit tests for cancellation races, leak checks with runtime.NumGoroutine, integration test against mock server that simulates slow flush and refused drain. - Benchmarks: measure Recv latency with and without inbound buffer for typical token sizes (1-3 tokens), and measure memory/goroutine usage under heavy concurrent streams.
risks_and_mitigation: - Risk: Server fleet may not support drain frames immediately -> mitigated by fallback to local timed drain and telemetry to detect server capability rollout. - Risk: Additional complexity in client could introduce regressions -> mitigate with feature-flagged rollout and canary in console. - Risk: Users relying on prior Close() blocking semantics (if any) -> default to immediate close for existing Close(); add GracefulClose opt-in.
progress_updates: 2025-02-10: RFC draft posted to internal design doc (link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Go+SDK+stream+drain+RFC).
2025-02-12: Spike implemented to verify reader goroutine pattern and backlog drain; initial unit tests added. Proof-of-concept shows no goroutine leaks when CloseImmediate is used.
2025-02-14: Implemented control-frame encoding and negotiated drain handshake; mock server accepts X-Drain header. Integration tests updated.

2025-02-16: Added WithReadDeadline API and tests for deadline override semantics. Observed a subtle race where parent context deadline could cancel before drain handshake acknowledged; added ordered cancel propagation to fix.
2025-02-18: PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/go-sdk/pull/812 (WIP). Running integration tests on CI.
testing_plan: - Unit tests: cancellation races (parent deadline while Recv in flight), GracefulClose with server accept/refuse drain, CloseImmediate behavior. - Leak tests: runtime.NumGoroutine snapshots before/after 10k short-lived streams. - Integration: run against mock server simulating 0 latency, slow flush, and connection loss. - E2E: enable canary in staging for a subset of customers for 24 hours, monitor error rates and goroutine growth. - QA checklist included in PR template.
release_plan: - Feature gated behind 'stream-drain' flag in SDK config. - Merge to main behind tests. - Canary rollout 1% of library downloads / client apps for 48h. - Monitor: goroutine count, stream error rates, drain-success ratio telemetry. - Full rollout after 2 canary cycles and no regression.
next_steps: 1) Finish PR fixes for race conditions and add leak-detector unit tests. 2) Add server capability discovery API so client can avoid handshake for older servers. 3) Write migration notes for customers using Close() in shutdown flows. 4) Schedule canary for 2025-02-25.
